ORDER ACCEPTING RELIABILITY BACKSTOP PROCUREMENT AND 
ESTABLISHING FURTHER PROCEDURES 
(Issued September 29, 2026) 
On July 31, 2026, as supplemented on August 14, 2026, PJM submitted proposed 
changes to its Open Access Transmission Tariff (OATT or Tariff) and Reliability 
Assurance Agreement (RAA),1 pursuant to section 205 of the Federal Power Act (FPA),2
to establish the Reliability Backstop Procurement (RBP).  The RBP is a one-time 
procurement of new capacity to address significant resource adequacy challenges 
primarily driven by an influx of large loads.3  As discussed below, we accept the 
proposed RBP for filing, suspend it for five months, effective February 28, 2027,    
subject to refund, and establish a paper hearing.  We also establish an FPA section 206 
proceeding.4
We find that certain aspects of PJM’s proposal are just and reasonable.  With 
respect to other aspects of PJM’s proposal that may be unjust and unreasonable, we direct 
further briefing regarding potential alternative approaches that the Commission believes

I.
Background 
PJM conducts a Base Residual Auction (BRA) to procure resource commitments 
sufficient to meet reliability requirements in the PJM region for a given delivery year, 
which spans from June 1 to May 31.5  The BRA and three Incremental Auctions are the 
Reliability Pricing Model (RPM) Auctions for a given delivery year. 
In December 2025, PJM announced that a BRA had cleared significantly below 
PJM’s reliability requirement for the first time in the auction’s history.  The 2027/2028 
BRA cleared 6,623 MW6 short of the reliability requirement, when also accounting for 
Fixed Resource Requirement (FRR) resources.7  The largest driver of the shortfall was 
5,250 MW of load growth forecast for that delivery year, nearly 5,100 MW of which was

II.
Filing 
On July 31, 2026, PJM submitted revisions to the Tariff and RAA to establish the 
RBP, a one-time procurement of new capacity to address resource adequacy challenges 
primarily driven by an influx of large loads.  According to PJM, the goal of the RBP is   
to obtain commitments of new RBP UCAP MW24 from eligible new resources, called 
RBP Resources, for a fixed term of up to 15 years, starting with the 2028/2029 delivery 
year at the earliest and ending no later than the 2042/2043 delivery year.25  PJM states 
that committing supply for terms of up to 15 years creates revenue certainty for the 
supply resources, generally can reduce financial and development risk, and may improve 
financing opportunities through lower capital costs or more favorable financing terms.26
Participants in the RBP are:  (1) sellers with RBP Sell Offers submitted on    
behalf of RBP Resources; and (2) PJMSettlement, Inc., acting as a counterparty on behalf 
of buyers, i.e., LSEs.27  PJM states that the RBP aims to procure capacity equal to the 
6,831 MW shortfall in the 2028/2029 BRA (Initial RBP Target), adjusted downward to 
reflect qualifying new capacity (Qualifying RBP Offset UCAP MW) serving new load 
and certain qualifying Electric Distributors that elect and meet requirements to opt out of 
the RBP (Opt-Out UCAP MW).  The Final RBP Target is the Initial RBP Target after 
downward adjustments.  Pursuant to the proposed Tariff provisions, new load is load that 
has an executed electric service agreement or transmission service agreement indicating 
that the load will come online during the 2027/2028 or 2028/2029 delivery year.28
To avoid double procurement, PJM proposes to require all available committed 
RBP UCAP MW to offer into the RPM Auctions as a price-taker, i.e., $0/MW-day 
UCAP, beginning with the first RPM Auction following the RBP commitment, for the 
applicable offered delivery year in which the term of the committed RBP UCAP MW

IV.
Discussion 
A.
Procedural Matters 
Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,        
18 C.F.R. § 385.214 (2025), the notices of intervention and timely, unopposed motions   
to intervene serve to make the entities that filed them parties to this proceeding. 
Rule 213(a)(2) of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. 
§ 385.213(a)(2) (2025), prohibits an answer to a protest or answer unless otherwise 
ordered by the decisional authority.  We accept the answers filed by AEP, the Kentucky 
Attorney General, EKPC, the Market Monitor, NJBPU, NOVEC, Voltus, PJM, P3, 
Constellation, PPL, Indicated PJM TOs, and FirstEnergy because they have provided 
information that assisted us in our decision-making process. 
B.
Substantive Matters 
Our preliminary analysis indicates that, while some aspects of PJM’s proposal are 
just and reasonable, other aspects of PJM’s proposal have not been shown to be just and 
reasonable and may be unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory or preferential, or 
otherwise unlawful.  PJM’s filing raises issues of material fact that cannot be resolved 
based on the record before us and that are more appropriately addressed in the paper 
hearing procedures established below.  Accordingly, we accept PJM’s proposal for filing 
and suspend it for five months to become effective February 28, 2027, subject to refund 
and to the outcome of paper hearing procedures.  Specifically, the paper hearing 
procedures should address the Commission’s potential modifications with respect to the 
portions of PJM’s existing RBP proposal that are discussed immediately below.  Aside 
from the three issues discussed directly below, we find that the other aspects of PJM’s 
RBP proposal are just and reasonable, as discussed in this order. 
We direct PJM to submit an initial brief addressing the paper hearing topics 
discussed below (cost allocation, Transmission Owner exit rules, and LSE collateral 
requirements), and to discuss in that brief whether its proposal could be just and 
reasonable if modified.  Other parties to this proceeding may also submit initial briefs    
on these topics.  Initial briefs are due 45 days from the date of this order.  However,       
we anticipate that the Commission would grant a motion to hold that briefing in this 
proceeding in abeyance if PJM submitted a new section 205 filing within 30 days from 
the date of this order.  Absent any such abeyance, responses to those initial briefs are due 
20 days after the date that initial briefs are due.  No additional answers or briefs will be 
permitted, and the Commission will look with great disfavor on any requests to extend

We anticipate that, following the paper hearing, the Commission may need to 
direct significant modifications to certain aspects of PJM’s proposal pursuant to its 
authority under section 205(e) of the FPA34 and Western Resources, Inc. v. FERC.35
Pursuant to Western Resources, the Commission may “transform” an existing  
FPA section 205 proceeding into an FPA section 206 proceeding and “impose its own 
rate,” provided the Commission makes three requisite findings:  (1) that the utility has 
failed to show that the proposed rate is just and reasonable, (2) that the existing rate is no 
longer just and reasonable, and (3) that the substitute rate established by the Commission 
is just and reasonable.36  We anticipate that, based on the record developed through the 
paper hearing, the Commission may find that each of these three prongs is satisfied and 
impose a new rate that incorporates some of the potential modifications discussed below.  
We first discuss why PJM’s existing rate may be unjust and unreasonable, then turn to 
why each aspect of PJM’s proposal that we are setting for paper hearing may be unjust 
and unreasonable, and then discuss why PJM’s proposal may be just and reasonable if 
modified.   
In addition to establishing paper hearing procedures under FPA section 205,       
this order also establishes a new FPA section 206 proceeding in anticipation of the 
Commission directing significant modifications to certain aspects of PJM’s RBP   
proposal following the paper hearing.  We institute this FPA section 206 proceeding 
because, as discussed in the next section below, PJM’s existing Tariff may be unjust and 
unreasonable.  When the Commission directs modifications under Western Resources,     
it does so by “transform[ing]” an existing section 205 proceeding into a section 206 
proceeding and making the requisite findings.  Though we are establishing an FPA 
section 206 proceeding today (Docket No. EL26-108), we are not instituting any further 
process under FPA section 206 at this time.

1.
PJM’s Existing Tariff May Be Unjust and Unreasonable 
We preliminarily find that PJM’s existing Tariff may be unjust and unreasonable 
because the existing reliability backstop provisions appear to be insufficient to prevent 
the grave resource adequacy concerns that led PJM to file the instant proposal in the first 
place.  We think it clear that PJM’s ordinary instrument for procuring sufficient capacity 
to meet PJM’s reliability requirement, the RPM, has failed to keep pace with the 
unprecedented influx of large load into the PJM Region in recent years.   
The existing Reliability Backstop Auction provision in PJM’s Tariff may be unjust 
and unreasonable because it has failed to remedy these reliability concerns.38  As PJM 
states, the Reliability Backstop Auction, which was proposed over 20 years ago and has 
never been used, was not designed to respond to the circumstances surrounding PJM’s 
current capacity shortfall.39  The Reliability Backstop Auction is triggered after three 
consecutive BRAs clear with a total unforced capacity amount that is more than one 
percent below PJM’s reserve margin.40  As stated above, PJM’s last two BRAs have 
cleared more than five percent below PJM’s reserve margin.  Moreover, once the 
Reliability Backstop Auction is triggered, PJM cannot run the auction until it “make[s] a 
filing with FERC for approval to conduct a Reliability Backstop Auction.”41

2.
Certain Aspects of PJM’s Proposal Are Just and Reasonable 
a.
Seller Eligibility Requirements, Sell Offers, and RPM 
Must-Offer Requirement 
i.
Filing 
Like offset capacity, RBP Resources (i.e., resources that bid into the RBP auction) 
must have never cleared in an RPM Auction and must have an expected in-service date 
by June 1, 2032.42  PJM, however, states that because RBP Resources have longer-term 
commitments and price certainty—as compared to resources that provide offset 
capacity—PJM proposes more restrictive criteria for RBP Resources to limit them to 
those resources that have demonstrated a high likelihood of success in reaching

Determination 
As a general matter, we find that PJM has demonstrated that its proposed 
eligibility requirements for RBP Resources are just and reasonable.  Specifically, we 
agree with PJM that its proposed eligibility requirements will limit RBP Resources to 
those resources that have demonstrated a high likelihood of success in reaching 
commercial operation and remaining available throughout the RBP commitment period, 
while not being so restrictive as to foreclose significant auction participation.  We further 
find that the stringency of the eligibility requirements for RBP Resources is reasonable 
given the revenue certainty that they will obtain over the RBP commitment period should 
they clear the RBP auction.   
We disagree with the Market Monitor that PJM should have attempted to match 
the duration of supply with the duration of data center demand.  The same energy must-
offer requirements apply to RBP Resources based on their resource type as would apply 
to any other resource of that type that cleared the RPM Auctions.  Similarly, we disagree 
with the Market Monitor’s arguments that uprates, Demand Resources, and DER 
Aggregation Resources should not be eligible RBP Resources.  The Commission has 
dismissed similar arguments from the Market Monitor in the context of the RPM.73
We acknowledge AEU’s concern that few Demand Resources and DER 
Aggregation Resources can lock in their customers for 15 years, as PJM’s proposal  
would require for them to qualify as RBP Resources.  We find, however, that PJM’s 
proposal is nonetheless reasonable.  As PJM explains, in return for the revenue certainty 
that participating in the RBP auction will provide, it is reasonable to expect these

Determination 
We are unpersuaded by arguments that PJM’s filing is unjust and unreasonable 
because it lacks locational constraints and direct market power mitigation.  First, we find 
that the proposal’s lack of locational constraints does not render PJM’s overall proposal 
unjust and unreasonable.  Specifically, the volume of capacity that PJM will procure 
through the RBP auction—up to 6,831 MW—is relatively small compared with total 
existing supply in PJM (149 GW), so even if RBP Resources are not located in the exact 
same Locational Deliverability Areas as new loads, the effect of any locational 
constraints should be limited.  Moreover, as PJM explains, the RBP is designed to 
address the PJM Region’s capacity shortfall, such that it is addressing an effectively 
region-wide problem.136  PIOs are correct that, depending on where RBP Resources 
choose to site themselves, significant Network Upgrades could be triggered.  But one can 
reasonably assume that RBP Resources will include anticipated Network Upgrade costs 
in their RBP Sell Offers—meaning that RBP Resources that anticipate significant 
Network Upgrade costs will be less likely to clear in the RBP auction. 
Second, we find that the lack of direct market power screens or mitigation for the 
RBP does not render PJM’s overall proposal unjust and reasonable.  As PJM explains, in 
the context of a pay-as-bid structure with a maximum willingness to pay set at $555/MW-
day, the effectiveness of such measures would be limited.  In addition, PJM’s proposed 
average-price cap of $555/MW-day further disciplines costs by increasing the risk that 
high offers do not clear.  And as PJM argues, the exercise of market power is unlikely if 
even a portion of the more than 130 GW of supply identified in the Charles River 
Associates Survey Results decides to participate and drive down prices.137

For purposes of determining whether a proposed cost allocation method is just and 
reasonable, both “[the Commission] and federal courts have long understood the [FPA’s] 
just-and-reasonable requirement ‘to incorporate a cost-causation principle.’”249  Under 
the cost causation principle, all Commission-jurisdictional rates and charges must “reflect 
to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer who must pay for them,”250 and 
costs must be allocated in a manner that is at least roughly commensurate with 
benefits.251  Compliance with this principle is evaluated by “comparing the costs assessed 
against a party to the burdens imposed or benefits drawn by that party.”252  Courts and the 
Commission have acknowledged that adherence to the cost causation principle does not 
require that cost allocation methods balance costs and benefits with “exacting 
precision.”253  Instead, the Commission may approve a given cost allocation framework if 
it “has an articulable and plausible reason to believe that the benefits are at least roughly 
commensurate with” the assigned costs.254  Consistent with this longstanding precedent, 
we apply the cost causation principle to evaluate PJM’s proposed method for allocating 
RBP costs.

SWETT, Chairman, concurring: 
American ratepayers and utilities need urgency, clarity, and discipline—none of 
which PJM appears capable of delivering at this time.  The Reliability Backstop 
Procurement proposal came before us on the last possible statutory day to open a 
procurement window on September 30.  Whether by accident or incompetence, that 
timing left the Commission no meaningful opportunity to issue a deficiency letter, seek 
additional record development, or establish hearing procedures to attempt to rehabilitate 
the mess we received.   
This Commission will not be forced into accepting a deeply flawed, eleventh-hour 
procurement mechanism with billion-dollar implications for consumers.  Today we triage 
the issues and urge PJM to promptly remedy them in a Federal Power Act Section 205 
filing.  We accept certain parts of the proposal that advance urgently needed capacity 
procurement, find that other components require reform, and provide guidance to inform 
expeditious resubmission. 
We are prepared to promptly act on a subsequent proposal that addresses the 
concerns raised in this order and meets the standards of the Federal Power Act.  The 
region’s reliability hangs in the balance.   
For these reasons, I respectfully concur.

ROSNER, Commissioner, concurring:  
I concur in today’s order because, at its core, our responsibility to the 67 million 
people in PJM is to keep the lights on.  While the record reflects a wide range of views on 
how best to address the emerging reliability challenges, the downside risk of inaction far 
outweighs the risk of an imperfect solution.  It is not a close call. 
The limited set of guidance we give PJM to revise its proposal will enable PJM to 
assign costs to those responsible (i.e. to the zones with data center growth) for the 
resource adequacy shortfall, consistent with cost causation principles, and it is my hope 
that PJM will act on this guidance swiftly so that needed generation may be procured.   
Many of the issues driving this filing extend beyond PJM’s jurisdiction to solve 
alone.  States and retail authorities must play an active role – particularly in establishing 
large-load retail tariffs, enforcing collateral requirements, and establishing clear rules for 
which customers should be curtailed first when circumstances require it (Hint: homes, 
hospitals, and schools should never be curtailed before data centers).  As the order 
acknowledges,1 these are decisions that sit squarely with states and their regulators, and 
meaningful progress requires their continued leadership. 
In the longer term PJM and its stakeholders must return to market fundamentals.  
Load and supply should have strong incentives to hedge, manage their risks, and procure 
the capacity they rely upon.  Market discipline – not ad hoc backstops – must again 
become the primary safeguard for reliability. 
For these reasons, while acknowledging the imperfections in the filing, I agree that 
taking action today is warranted, and I respectfully concur. 
For these reasons, I respectfully concur.

SEE, Commissioner, concurring: 
PJM needs more generation: Soaring electricity demand from data centers, 
artificial intelligence, domestic manufacturing, and other strategic industries continues to 
challenge a region that faces increasingly tight supply.  Meeting that demand requires 
sufficient generation, including dependable resources that support the system around the 
clock.  PJM must move fast to secure the resources to serve its growing system. 
But how PJM—really, PJM’s ratepayers—pays for those resources matters.  As I 
have said before, customers that drive new costs should bear appropriate responsibility 
for them.  Existing customers should not be left paying costs attributable to new demand.  
That principle is particularly important here where PJM proposes a backstop procurement 
specifically to deal with the capacity shortfall that rapid load growth largely drove. 
PJM needs urgent action and this mechanism, the RBP, can be a critical tool to 
bring additional capacity to the region.  Unfortunately, though, PJM missed the mark on 
an important element of its proposal: it did not adequately ensure that the procurement’s 
costs will be allocated to the customers who drive its need. 
Today’s order is not perfect; the filing it responds to, even less.  But today the 
Commission provides PJM a path forward to solve what its current proposal lacks when it 
comes to fair cost allocation.  PJM should move quickly to take it. 
That work must include a serious focus on load forecasting.  After years of 
relatively flat electricity demand, regulators and grid operators need to adjust to sustained 
and asymmetric growth.  That means better load forecasts, a clearer picture of which 
projects will materialize, and enough generation and infrastructure to serve them.  Better 
information about where, when, and why load is growing also provides a stronger 
foundation for determining who should bear the costs associated with serving that 
growth. 
PJM does not have the luxury of standing still.  The region needs additional 
generation, and I encourage PJM to swiftly return to the Commission with a section 205 
filing we can accept so that the procurement can move forward quickly.  In doing so, 
PJM must better ensure that the customers driving new costs bear appropriate 
responsibility for them and that existing customers are not left paying the bill instead. 
For these reasons, I respectfully concur.

LACERTE, Commissioner, concurring:  
I concur in today’s order but write separately as a reminder of what this order   
is—or should be—about.  Reliability Backstop Procurement is designed to make sure the 
costs of the large load at issue here are appropriately allocated to that load and not to 
other consumers and, in that vein, it is also an attempt to get new assets onto the PJM grid 
in a time of desperate need.   
This is not a problem with an exceedingly easy or even single solution.  While a 
perfect solution may not exist, it does not mean this is an unsolvable problem.  
This moment must be met.  We must do so not only because it is one of the many 
vital issues we are presented with in PJM and other regions of this country, but because it 
is important for Americans to do so.   
The vital nature of the large load integration issue to all Americans is highlighted 
by the very existence of the January 2026 Statement of Principles Regarding PJM1 in 
which the White House National Energy Dominance Council and the governors of all 13 
PJM states joined together to address these large load issues as well as the March 2026, 
White House Ratepayer Protection Pledge which addressed that new large loads will, at a 
minimum, “build, bring, or buy the new generation resources and electricity needed to 
satisfy their new energy demands, paying the full cost of those resources”2 and which 
received broad consensus from utilities, cooperatives, data center developers, and 
governors.3

What all of this tells me is that time is of the essence.  While we could orbit these 
issues in additional briefings that would cause additional delay to the reliability backstop 
auction and the hope for relief it provides. 
PJM:  you must take action.  You alone have the ability to resolve the outstanding 
issues in the most time efficient manner by making a section 205 filing under the 
timelines set forth in this order—or sooner—that thoughtfully addresses the infirmities of 
the original filing addressed in this order.  Do not deviate from the principles of ratepayer 
protection in that filing.  
A competent and effective RTO can take this half-baked cake and finish the job.  
Does PJM meet that description?  They’re on the clock.  
For these reasons, I respectfully concur.
